title: Laptop hardware: what's different and why it matters
summary: SODIMM, M.2, and the parts you'll actually be asked to replace.
body:
## Everything is smaller, and that's the whole story

A laptop is a desktop with the same jobs and none of the room. Almost every A+ laptop question comes down to knowing the *small-form-factor* version of a part you already recognize.

### Memory

Laptops use **SODIMM** (Small Outline DIMM) rather than the full-length DIMMs desktops use. They're physically shorter and keyed differently, so you can't accidentally fit a desktop stick.

- **DDR4 SODIMM** — 260 pins
- **DDR5 SODIMM** — 262 pins

The pin counts differ from their desktop cousins (DDR4 DIMM is 288 pins), so a slot only accepts one generation. If a memory upgrade won't seat, the first suspect is a **generation or form-factor mismatch**, not a bad module.

### Storage

Modern laptops overwhelmingly use **M.2** drives. Two things trip people up:

- **M.2 is a form factor, not an interface.** An M.2 slot can carry either **SATA** or **NVMe** signaling. A drive and slot can physically fit and still not work if the slot only wired one of the two.
- **Keying** (the notch position — B key, M key, B+M) tells you what a slot supports. An NVMe drive is usually M-keyed; a SATA M.2 is often B+M.

### The parts you actually replace

Field-replaceable on most laptops: RAM, the M.2 or 2.5" drive, the **battery**, the **Wi-Fi card**, and sometimes the keyboard. The **display assembly** — panel, backlight, and often the antenna and webcam — is treated as one unit; you rarely replace the panel alone.

> Exam habit: when a laptop symptom involves wireless, remember the **Wi-Fi antenna wires run up through the hinges into the display bezel**. A screen replacement that leaves Wi-Fi weak usually means an antenna lead wasn't reconnected.

### Display technologies

You'll be asked to compare panel types:

- **TN** — fastest response, cheapest, worst color and viewing angles.
- **IPS** — best color accuracy and viewing angles, slightly slower.
- **VA** — best contrast, a middle ground on everything else.
- **OLED** — per-pixel lighting, true blacks, risk of burn-in.

And know that the **inverter** (which powered older CCFL backlights) is a legacy concept — LED-backlit panels don't use one, so a modern dim-screen problem points at the backlight LEDs or the panel, not an inverter.

title: Mobile connectivity: cellular, Bluetooth, and hotspots
summary: The radios in a phone and the settings that break them.
body:
## Three radios, three failure modes

Mobile devices juggle several radios at once, and A+ likes to test whether you can tell which one a symptom belongs to.

### Cellular

- A **SIM** (or eSIM) identifies the device to the carrier. "No SIM" or "not registered" errors point here.
- **Airplane mode** kills *all* radios at once. It's the single fastest way to explain "nothing wireless works, everything else is fine."
- **PRL** (Preferred Roaming List) and baseband/radio firmware updates are carrier-side fixes for a phone that connects but can't get data.

### Bluetooth

Bluetooth has to be **paired** before it works, and pairing is where problems live:

1. Make the device **discoverable**.
2. Initiate pairing from the other device.
3. Confirm the **PIN or passkey** if prompted.
4. Test the connection.

If a previously working device won't reconnect, **removing (forgetting) the pairing and re-pairing** clears most stale-pairing faults.

### Hotspots and tethering

A phone can share its cellular data three ways:

- **Wi-Fi hotspot** — the phone becomes an access point.
- **Bluetooth tethering** — slower, but very low power.
- **USB tethering** — fastest and charges the phone at the same time.

> Exam habit: "hotspot works but the laptop can't reach it" is usually the hotspot's **maximum connected-device limit** or a **band mismatch** (an older laptop that only sees 2.4 GHz while the hotspot broadcasts 5 GHz).

title: Ports and protocols worth memorizing
summary: The port numbers A+ asks about, grouped so they stick.
body:
## Learn them in pairs and groups, not as a flat list

Rote-memorizing 20 port numbers is miserable and doesn't stick. Group them by what they do.

### Web and its secure twin

| Service | Port | Note |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | 80 | Plain web |
| HTTPS | 443 | TLS-encrypted web |

Almost every "secure version" rides a different port — this pairing is the pattern to internalize.

### Remote access

| Service | Port | Note |
|---|---|---|
| SSH | 22 | Encrypted remote shell |
| Telnet | 23 | **Unencrypted** — legacy, avoid |
| RDP | 3389 | Windows Remote Desktop |

SSH (22) and Telnet (23) sit right next to each other and do the same job; the exam loves that SSH is the secure one.

### Mail

| Service | Port | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| SMTP | 25 | Sending |
| POP3 | 110 | Retrieving (download) |
| IMAP | 143 | Retrieving (sync) |

### Naming, addressing, and file sharing

| Service | Port |
|---|---|
| DNS | 53 |
| DHCP | 67 / 68 |
| SMB (file sharing) | 445 |
| LDAP | 389 |

> Exam habit: **DNS is 53**. It shows up constantly, both as a port question and as the answer to "I can reach a site by IP but not by name." Burn 53 into memory first.

title: IP addressing and what APIPA is telling you
summary: Private ranges, DHCP, and reading 169.254 as a diagnosis.
body:
## An address is a diagnosis

The single most useful networking skill for the exam — and the job — is reading an IP address as a clue about what went wrong.

### Private ranges (RFC 1918)

These never route on the public internet; a home or office LAN uses them behind NAT:

- **10.0.0.0** – 10.255.255.255 (a /8)
- **172.16.0.0** – 172.31.255.255 (a /12)
- **192.168.0.0** – 192.168.255.255 (a /16)

Seeing one of these on a client is normal and expected.

### APIPA — the address that means "DHCP failed"

If a client is set to obtain an address automatically but **can't reach a DHCP server**, it assigns itself one from:

> **169.254.0.0 – 169.254.255.255**

This is **APIPA** (Automatic Private IP Addressing). An APIPA address is a symptom, not a setting. It means:

- The DHCP server is down or unreachable, **or**
- A cable/switch problem is cutting the client off from it, **or**
- The client and server are on different segments with no DHCP relay.

A machine with a 169.254 address can talk to *other* APIPA machines on the same segment but has no gateway and no DNS — so "local network works, internet doesn't" with a 169.254 address is a classic DHCP-failure signature.

### Loopback

**127.0.0.1** (IPv4) always refers to the local machine. Pinging it tests that the TCP/IP stack itself is alive — if that fails, the problem is the OS's networking, not any cable.

### Static vs dynamic

Most clients get addresses from **DHCP**. Servers, printers, and network gear are often **static** (or DHCP reservations) so their address never changes. A printer that "moves" and breaks everyone's print queue is usually a static device that got a DHCP address, or vice versa.

title: RAID levels and what each one is buying you
summary: 0, 1, 5, 10 — the trade between speed, redundancy, and capacity.
body:
## Every RAID level is a trade

RAID combines multiple drives into one logical volume. Each level trades among three things: **speed**, **redundancy**, and **usable capacity**. Know what each one sacrifices.

### RAID 0 — striping

Data is split across drives, so reads and writes are fast. **No redundancy at all** — if any one drive dies, the whole array is lost.

- Minimum drives: 2
- Usable capacity: 100%
- Fault tolerance: **none**

RAID 0 is pure performance. The name is a trap — "0" means zero redundancy.

### RAID 1 — mirroring

Every drive holds an identical copy. Survives a drive failure with no data loss.

- Minimum drives: 2
- Usable capacity: 50%
- Fault tolerance: one drive

### RAID 5 — striping with parity

Data and **parity** are spread across all drives. Can rebuild after **one** drive fails using the parity.

- Minimum drives: 3
- Usable capacity: (n − 1) drives
- Fault tolerance: one drive

RAID 5 is the classic "balanced" choice — good capacity, good reads, survives one failure.

### RAID 10 — a mirror of stripes

Combines 1 and 0: mirrored pairs that are then striped. Fast **and** redundant, at the cost of half your capacity.

- Minimum drives: 4
- Usable capacity: 50%
- Fault tolerance: one drive per mirrored pair

> Exam habit: match the level to the *requirement in the question*. "Maximum performance, data is disposable" → **0**. "Survive a drive failure, only two drives" → **1**. "Balance capacity and redundancy across several drives" → **5**. "Best of both, budget allows" → **10**.

title: Power supplies: wattage, rails, and connectors
summary: Sizing a PSU and the connectors you have to recognize.
body:
## The part most likely to kill other parts

A failing power supply doesn't just stop working — it can behave intermittently and take other components with it. A+ expects you to size one correctly and recognize its connectors.

### Wattage: add up the load, then leave headroom

The PSU has to supply the **sum** of everything's draw, with margin. The single biggest consumer in most builds is the **GPU**, which is why a new graphics card is the most common reason an existing PSU becomes inadequate.

Signs of an **undersized or failing** PSU:

- Random reboots or shutdowns **under load** (gaming, rendering) but stable at idle
- The system won't POST with a new high-draw card installed
- Capacitor/coil noise or a burning smell

> Exam habit: "stable at idle, reboots under load, just added a GPU" is almost always **insufficient PSU wattage** or **missing PCIe power connectors** — not RAM, not the drive.

### Connectors to recognize

| Connector | Powers |
|---|---|
| 24-pin (20+4) | Motherboard main power |
| 8-pin (4+4) EPS | CPU power |
| 6/8-pin PCIe | Graphics card |
| SATA power | Drives, some fans |
| Molex | Legacy peripherals |

A modern GPU needs **specific 6- or 8-pin PCIe connectors** — verify both the total wattage *and* that the PSU has the right connectors before an upgrade.

### Voltage and safety

A PSU with a **voltage selector switch** (115V / 230V) must match the wall supply — the wrong setting damages hardware. And because PSUs hold charge, they're on the short list of parts you **don't open**; you replace them as a unit.

title: Cloud models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and the shared responsibility line
summary: Who manages what, and where your responsibility starts.
body:
## The difference is *who manages what*

The cloud service models are a single idea seen at three depths: the more the provider manages, the less you control — and the less you're responsible for.

### IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service

The provider gives you **virtual hardware**: compute, storage, networking. You install and manage the OS and everything above it. Think of a bare virtual machine you're handed the keys to.

*You manage:* OS, patches, runtime, apps, data.

### PaaS — Platform as a Service

The provider manages the OS and runtime; you just deploy **your application and data**. You don't patch the server — you push code.

*You manage:* your app, your data.

### SaaS — Software as a Service

The provider manages **everything**; you just use the finished software through a browser. Email like Microsoft 365, or a CRM, are SaaS.

*You manage:* your data and your user accounts, essentially nothing else.

> A one-line mnemonic: **IaaS = you get a server, PaaS = you get a platform, SaaS = you get software.** Each step up hands more of the stack to the provider.

### Deployment models

Separately from *what* is delivered, there's *where*:

- **Public cloud** — shared provider infrastructure (AWS, Azure).
- **Private cloud** — dedicated to one organization.
- **Hybrid** — a mix, with workloads moving between them.
- **Community** — shared by organizations with common needs.

### Other terms A+ uses

- **Elasticity / rapid scaling** — resources grow and shrink on demand.
- **Measured service** — you pay for exactly what you use (metered).
- **Resource pooling** — many customers share one physical pool, isolated logically.
- **High availability** — the service survives individual component failures.

title: The six-step troubleshooting methodology
summary: The process A+ tests directly — in order, and why the order matters.
body:
## The exam tests the *order*, not just the steps

This is the single most reliably tested procedure on the exam, and questions almost always hinge on **what comes next** from a given point. Learn it as a sequence.

### The six steps

1. **Identify the problem.** Gather information, question the user, and — critically — **back up before making changes**. Reproduce the problem if you can.
2. **Establish a theory of probable cause.** Question the obvious. Consider everything from the simplest explanation up.
3. **Test the theory to determine the cause.** If the theory is confirmed, move on. If not, form a new theory — or **escalate**.
4. **Establish a plan of action** to resolve the problem, and implement it.
5. **Verify full system functionality** and, if applicable, implement **preventive measures** so it doesn't recur.
6. **Document** findings, actions, and outcomes.

### Why each boundary matters

- **Backing up sits in step 1**, before any change. This catches people out — the temptation is to jump to a fix, but the methodology puts data protection first.
- **Testing the theory (3) comes before the plan (4).** You don't build a fix around a guess; you confirm the cause first. "You have a theory, what next?" is *test it*, not *fix it*.
- **Verify (5) comes before document (6).** You confirm the fix actually worked before you write it up — documenting a fix you never verified is how a "resolved" ticket bounces back.

> Exam habit: when a question drops you at one step and asks for the next, don't reason from the technical situation — recite the sequence. The answer is whatever step follows, every time.

title: Reading POST failures and boot problems
summary: Beeps, no-POST, and where a boot actually dies.
body:
## Where in the boot did it die?

Boot problems feel chaotic until you place *where* the failure happened. A machine powers on, runs **POST** (Power-On Self-Test), hands off to the **boot device**, then loads the OS. Each stage fails differently.

### No power at all

No lights, no fans. Work outward from the wall: power cable, PSU switch and voltage selector, the motherboard power connectors, then the power button header. This is a **power delivery** problem, not a boot problem.

### Powers on, no display, no POST

Fans spin but nothing appears and it never beeps normally. Suspect the parts POST checks first:

- **RAM** — reseat it; a single stick in the first slot is the classic isolation test.
- **GPU / display** — reseat, confirm the monitor and cable.
- **CPU / motherboard** — last, and hardest.

**POST beep codes** and motherboard diagnostic LEDs tell you which subsystem failed before video is even available. A repeating memory beep pattern points straight at RAM.

### POSTs, but can't find an OS

You see POST, then **"No boot device"**, "Operating system not found," or **"Inaccessible boot device."** POST passed, so the hardware basics are fine — the problem is between firmware and OS:

- Wrong **boot order** in UEFI/BIOS (booting an empty USB or the wrong disk).
- The boot drive isn't detected — a **loose SATA/power cable** or a failed drive.
- Corrupt bootloader or partition table.

### Boots, then fails loading Windows

Getting into the bootloader and then failing — a **BSOD**, a boot loop, or **"Bootmgr is missing"** — is an OS-level problem (drivers, corrupt system files, a bad update), not hardware. This is where Startup Repair and Safe Mode come in.

> Exam habit: the diagnostic question is always **"how far did it get?"** No POST → hardware POST checks (RAM/GPU/CPU). POSTs but no OS → boot order and the drive. Loads Windows and crashes → the OS. Placing the failure narrows the cause before you touch anything.
